# On the Strange Comfort of Incomplete Things

I've been thinking lately about how we live surrounded by unfinished business, and how rarely we acknowledge this as simply the human condition rather than a personal failing. There's something peculiar about modern life—a constant low-level anxiety that stems not from any single catastrophe, but from the ambient awareness that nothing is ever truly complete. We exist in a perpetual state of almost-done.

Consider the average person's relationship with their home. I don't mean people who are genuinely struggling with housing insecurity—that's a different conversation, and a real crisis. I mean the ordinary middle-class person who has a roof and walls and yet experiences their dwelling as somehow perpetually inadequate. The kitchen could use better organization. The bedroom would be better with different lighting. Those baseboards have needed painting for three years. There are boxes in the closet from a move that happened five years ago. There are plants that are mostly dead but occasionally you water them and they spring back to life, so you can't quite justify throwing them away.

We've internalized the idea that spaces should be "done"—that there's some final state where a home is complete, perfect, requiring no further thought. This is, I think, a relatively new delusion. For most of human history, homes were works in perpetual progress. You fixed the roof when it leaked. You added a room when the family grew. You maintained what you had. The idea that a space could be finished, that you could achieve some state of domestic perfection and then simply enjoy it forever, is a luxury good masquerading as a universal standard.

I think about this when I scroll through interior design photos online—those perfectly staged rooms where nothing is out of place, no book is askew on its shelf, no mug sits next to a sink. These aren't homes. They're photographs of homes. Or rather, they're photographs of the idea of homes, which is a different thing entirely. A real home is a record of living. It's incomplete by necessity.

The same applies to our interior lives, though we seem even less willing to admit this. We're supposed to have our careers figured out by thirty, preferably by twenty-five. We're supposed to know what we want to be and become it. We're supposed to complete projects—both literal and metaphorical—and move on to the next thing. But ask anyone honest about their life, and you'll find an enormous catalog of begun-but-not-finished endeavors. The novel that got to page sixty and stalled. The language learning app that's been gathering dust for two years (though you paid for the subscription). The exercise routine that worked for three weeks. The ambitious project you were going to tackle during the pandemic and somehow never quite managed.

I wonder if we'd be happier if we reframed these not as failures but as the texture of a life actually lived. There's something almost holy about the person who reads many books rather than few, who starts many projects rather than completing a few perfect ones. This person is engaged with the world, curious, testing things out, seeing what they might become interested in. The "failure to complete" is actually a form of experimentation.

There's also something I've noticed about people who are genuinely accomplished in some field—whether it's writing or music or painting or building things. They almost universally report that the work never feels finished. The novel that got published still feels incomplete to them. The song that thousands of people love still feels like it could be better. This isn't false modesty, I think. It's genuine. The deeper you go into any domain, the more you understand how much there is to know, how many choices you made that could have been made differently, how many ways the thing could be better. Completion is a luxury of ignorance.

Maybe the problem isn't that we have too many incomplete things. Maybe it's that we shame ourselves for it instead of accepting it as natural. We're supposed to finish what we start. We're supposed to have discipline, follow-through, grit. These are fine qualities, but they're not the only qualities. There's also the quality of being comfortable with exploration, with trying things, with learning through doing rather than planning exhaustively before beginning.

I think about my own writing this way. I have a document on my computer with fragments—ideas that came to me while I was doing something else, passages that felt true in the moment, images I wanted to preserve. Some of these fragments are years old. Are they failures? Have I failed to write the full pieces they belong to? Or are they seeds, waiting for the right conditions to grow? Some probably will never become anything. And that's fine. They served their purpose when they were written. They captured something true about how the world looked on a particular day, and that has value whether or not it gets woven into a larger whole.

I wonder if one of the things that makes modern life particularly anxious is that we've extended the logic of completion into domains where it doesn't belong. A novel should probably have an ending. A bridge should probably be finished before people drive on it. But a life? A creative practice? A relationship? These aren't things that get finished. They're things that you inhabit, day by day, making small adjustments, learning and growing, sometimes doubling back to refine something you thought was settled.

There's a particular kind of person I notice who seems to have less anxiety about these things—not because they're inherently less anxious, but because they've made peace with incompletion. They tend to be people who have some field where they actively practice their incompleteness. Musicians are often like this. They'll pick up their instrument and play the same piece for twenty years, never feeling like they've "finished" learning it. Each time is a new attempt, a new understanding, a new appreciation of what the piece contains. They've externalized their incompletion into their art form, and somehow this seems to make it easier for them to accept incompletion in other areas of life.

I've been trying to think of what incompleteness looks like in a healthy form. Not the anxiety of half-done things nagging at you, making you feel lazy and inefficient, but the openness of knowing that everything you care about is still being discovered, still revealing new dimensions. Maybe it's the difference between incomplete and unfinished. Incomplete things are still in process. Unfinished things are things you failed to complete. The emotional valence is entirely different.

There's a phrase I keep coming back to: "in progress." It's what artists put on their work when it's not done but it's being shown anyway. "Work in progress." "In progress" suggests movement, directionality, ongoing engagement. It's honest about the state of things without being apologetic about it.

I think most of life is "in progress." Your personality is in progress. Your understanding of what you believe is in progress. Your skill at being a parent, a partner, a friend—all in progress. Your attempt to be a good person is definitely in progress, and probably always will be. The moral arc of an individual doesn't end until you die, and maybe not even then, if you believe in anything that happens after.

What would it mean to embrace this more fully? To stop waiting for some future state where you've finally figured things out, finally finished improving yourself, finally completed the important project? To instead notice and appreciate the strange privilege of being a being who can still learn, still change, still discover new things about yourself and the world?

I'm reading a lot of climate literature at the moment, and it's made me think about incompletion in yet another way. We live in a time when we're asked to care about problems—climate change, social injustice, democratic erosion—that will not be solved in our lifetimes. Possibly not in several lifetimes. How do you sustain commitment to work that will not be finished, that you will not see completed, that might in fact only get worse before it gets better (if it gets better at all)?

The only way I can figure out is to stop seeing the completion as the point. The point becomes the work itself, the daily commitment, the incremental improvement, the community of people also working on it. You become a person who does these things, not a person working toward finishing these things. And that's strangely freeing, even in the context of genuinely serious problems.

There's something almost beautiful about the idea of being a custodian rather than a finisher. A custodian maintains, cares for, passes on to the next person. A forest ranger isn't trying to finish the forest. A librarian isn't trying to finish the library. A teacher isn't trying to finish education. They're tending to something that will continue beyond them, and there's dignity in that role.

Maybe one of the secret joys of getting older is realizing that you're not supposed to finish. You're supposed to show up and tend to the things you care about, and then other people will tend to them after you, and that's how the world actually works. The cathedrals of Europe took centuries to build. No individual architect finished them. But each one did their part, did their best with the materials and understanding available to them, and passed it on.

I notice I'm most peaceful when I'm thinking about my life this way. When I'm not tracking toward some imaginary finish line. When I'm instead focused on being the kind of person who does the kinds of things I think are worth doing. When I'm tending to my relationships, my work, my curious engagement with ideas, not because it will all be done someday, but because that's what the tending itself offers me.

The boxes in my closet from that move? I'm probably going to open them someday and deal with them. Or maybe I won't, and whoever cleans out my apartment after I die will do it. And that's okay. It doesn't mean my apartment is a failure. It's just real. It's just the way a life actually looks, with its incomplete things and its slow accumulations and its gentle neglect of non-urgent business.

I'm trying to bring this same grace to my creative projects, my self-improvement attempts, my half-learned skills. I'm trying to see the incompletion not as a character flaw but as a sign that I'm alive and engaged, that there are more things I want to learn and try than I have time for, which seems like a good problem to have. I'm trying to write from the space of "still learning" rather than "not yet good enough." They're the same statement, but the emotional quality is completely different.

This is what I've been thinking about lately: the strange comfort of incomplete things. The way everything I care about is still becoming. The way I myself am still becoming. The way that might be exactly as it should be, and the only real failing would be to stop showing up for it.
